A standard state-space setup for a dynamic hedge ratio writes 
 yₜ = xₜβₜ + vₜ 
 βₜ = βₜ₋₁ + wₜ
 where vₜ ∼ N(0, R) and wₜ ∼ N(0, Q). 
The Kalman filter estimates βₜ recursively and adapts on its own to slow drift in the relationship.

In a pairs setting the spread is usually sₜ = yₜ − xₜβ̂ₜ, and trade P&L gets computed as s_exit − s_entry. Here is the problem. If β̂ₜ keeps updating between entry and exit, the measured P&L splits into two pieces: a true price-return component, and a parameter-adaptation component proportional to (β̂_entry − β̂_exit)·x_exit. The second piece is not tradeable. It is the filter moving the goalposts.

What goes wrong from there is subtle. A filter can explain away a structural break by re-centering the spread around a moving equilibrium, so the backtest never sees the break at all. Win rates come out high and drawdowns come out shallow, and a good share of both is coming from changes in β̂ₜ rather than from prices actually converging.

Two approaches deal with it. One freezes the hedge ratio for the life of each trade, so the P&L is pure price return and the adaptation term is zero by design; the cost is a stale hedge on longer holds. The other lets the filter keep updating but decomposes the backtest P&L into its price and adaptation components, and counts only the first as evidence the strategy works. Either way, break detection moves to the innovations, eₜ = yₜ − xₜβ̂ₜ⁻, where β̂ₜ⁻ is the one-step-ahead prediction, and a CUSUM on eₜ catches persistent one-sided deviations. The filter stays an estimator instead of becoming a hidden source of P&L.

Not a fan of Kalman filters in a financial setting. They are well suited to tracking trajectories with well behaved physical dynamics estimated with noisy measurements and corrected based on evidence. But the problem is that financial markets don’t exhibit well behaved physical dynamics. At best, the microstructure of order books and order flows give you the mechanical physics of price formation and potential evolution. But nothing guarantees a stable book configuration, nor stable order flows. But I think one has a better chance modeling that than prices, which are really an antecedent byproduct of the process. Unfortunately, all filters one might propose are causal. The stability of your modal frequencies and the predictability of phase variation are the underlying necessary conditions for success. I’ve learned to evaluate everything on that type of econometric predicate when calibrating a model.

I found that in this space that phase shifts revealed very precise information about the relationships between temporal delays and modulation in frequency and amplitude. Clearly you don’t want noise to contaminate the filter, nor does one want stochastic non-structural mid frequency transients to bias the parameters estimates. Yes, the observation equation deliberately excludes αₜ. The specification yₜ = xₜβₜ + vₜ, with a single latent state βₜ follows a random walk, βₜ = βₜ₋₁ + wₜ. Any reversion in the pair is left to appear in the residual, which is what the strategy trades. A time-varying αₜ would compete with the residual for the same variation and, over time, absorb much of what would otherwise be the spread, leaving less that is tradeable.

Excluding αₜ also preserves break detection. A level shift the model cannot immediately accommodate shows up as persistent one-sided innovations eₜ = yₜ − xₜβ̂ₜ⁻, which is what the CUSUM monitors. With αₜ included as a state, the filter can instead re-center the relationship and mask the shift.

There is also an identification consideration. When xₜ is highly persistent, a moving intercept and the term βₜxₜ become difficult to distinguish statistically, so the decomposition between them is unstable. In this setup, drift large enough to matter is treated as a signal to exit rather than something the model keeps absorbing.

Love the graphic, but isn't this ultimately a P&L-accounting error for a single entry trade? I accept that your exit timing is a function of the adapted beta, but P&L remains the sum of the price changes across the positions actually held, plus carry and costs. For a single-entry trade, there is only one set of entry quantities and the exit value of the spread is exactly y_exit - B_entry*x_exit. If one rebalances dynamically, then one sums the period P&Ls based on the actual changing holdings. So unless the beta updates are traded, they cannot generate P&L. The 'adaptation PnL' is thus a change in estimate spread rather than economic decomposition of PnL. A direct analogy is an options desk. They first calculate the actual single-period P&Ls from positions held during that period and then use Greeks to explain it, rather than the other way around.

Freezing the hedge ratio creates basis risk, but it also gives the trade a clean invalidation point. That trade off is preferable to allowing the model to quietly redefine equilibrium during a drawdown. A stale hedge is visible and measurable because a moving target can conceal genuine thesis failure until the loss reaches live capital.
